content: Clinical and administrative practices must encompass measures to protect, promote, and support breastfeeding, alongside the responsibilities of health workers as outlined in the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes. Updating curricula, particularly national ones, is a complex and time-consuming process that involves multiple stakeholders, such as ministries of education, higher learning institutions, and professional credentialing organizations, many of whom may not typically engage in breastfeeding-related activities. Pre-service training is essential for long-term improvements in maternity care practices. However, health professionals already in practice who work with pregnant women, mothers, and infants must also receive education on providing timely and appropriate care. Continuing education and in-service training are critical until a sufficient number of newly trained professionals across all relevant disciplines have graduated. Where national guidelines or curricula for in-service training exist, they must integrate clinical practices and the Code to ensure consistency and avoid the need for individual facilities to develop their own materials. Many countries have adapted the 20-hour course from the 2009 Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI) implementation guidance. WHO and UNICEF are revising this course to align with updated Ten Steps and Global Standards and are developing an Integrated Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) Counseling Training package. In-service training should be viewed as a short-term solution rather than a permanent method for capacity development. Regular refresher training sessions and continuing education, delivered in modular formats, can minimize disruptions to service provision. Training should focus on competency-based approaches, emphasizing practical skills over theoretical knowledge. Teaching staff in relevant schools and universities, as well as trainers involved in in-service training and continuing education, must be trained in the new materials. This investment is crucial for sustainable capacity strengthening and is a key responsibility of the national breastfeeding coordination body. A train-the-trainer approach can efficiently create a large cadre of BFHI experts nationwide, disseminating in-depth knowledge about the Ten Steps in a cost-effective manner. Educational materials for appropriate maternity and newborn care can be delivered through electronic or online courses, offering an efficient and low-cost method of education. This approach allows health professionals to learn at their own pace and revisit information as needed. However, some skills require face-to-face interaction for effective teaching and assessment. Staff may also benefit from group learning sessions to process challenging personal experiences or address situations where evidence-based care was not feasible. Direct observation is necessary for skills assessment, necessitating one-on-one learning and competency-based evaluations. Facility managers play a critical role in protecting, promoting, and supporting breastfeeding in maternity and newborn care settings. Performance-based contracts with specific breastfeeding targets can enhance accountability. Managers must have a thorough understanding of breastfeeding and the BFHI to guide and oversee its implementation effectively. Educating facility administrators and medical directors, combined with technical assistance, can drive changes in practices. Implementing most BFHI standards does not necessarily incur additional costs and may even save money after initial investments in new practices. External assessment systems should be used to regularly evaluate adherence to the Ten Steps. Facilities providing maternity and newborn services are responsible for delivering care in line with Baby-Friendly guidelines and national evidence-based quality standards. While internal monitoring mechanisms are essential, external assessments are critical for quality assurance. These assessments should focus on facilitating technical assistance and correcting inappropriate practices. External assessors may report findings to a designated group, which then provides feedback to the facility. External monitors can validate results and identify gaps in care more effectively than internal staff. Countries must maintain ongoing external assessment processes, including assessments and re-assessments, to validate adherence to the Ten Steps and provide feedback for improvement. External assessments should integrate with other quality-assurance processes, such as facility certification or health insurance assessments. In some systems, achieving Baby-Friendly designation fulfills certain quality assurance criteria, reducing certification costs. Incorporating BFHI clinical standards into facility certification procedures can institutionalize these practices and lower overall program costs. Assessment of the Ten Steps includes both clinical and administrative evaluations, and additional training may be required to integrate BFHI assessments into existing systems. External assessments should review documentation on key clinical practice indicators, including sentinel indicators, and validate facility monitoring data through interviews with staff, pregnant women, and mothers. Regular external assessments, conducted at least every five years, are recommended, with more frequent evaluations preferred. The depth and frequency of these assessments depend on the quality and frequency of internal monitoring and the information reported to higher levels. In some cases, a reduced set of indicators may be selected for integration into other certification or quality-assurance systems. At a minimum, sentinel indicators on early initiation of breastfeeding and exclusive breastfeeding rates during hospital stays should be included, as breastfeeding should be the norm in all maternity and newborn care. If integration into other quality-assessment systems is insufficient to ensure compliance with breastfeeding standards, a standalone vertical assessment can be developed. While vertical assessments may include more specific breastfeeding indicators, they can be more costly and challenging to sustain long-term. Alternatively, spot checks may be used. An adequately resourced department within the Ministry of Health could manage an external assessment system. Embedding it within existing professional organizations or well-functioning NGOs may also be an option in certain settings. Incentives and sanctions can be developed to encourage compliance with the Ten Steps. Healthcare facilities make policy decisions based on various factors, including scientific evidence, recommendations, regulations, costs, client satisfaction, and public perceptions. National programs should consider appropriate incentives or sanctions to drive necessary changes in maternity and newborn care facilities to fully protect, promote, and support breastfeeding. Incentives for public and private facilities may differ. Performance-based financing, where meeting standards financially benefits the facility, is one option. Facilities with deficiencies in practices may receive lower reimbursement rates per delivery compared to those in full compliance. This model, known as performance-based financing or payment-for-performance, is increasingly used to incentivize quality and efficiency. While it may not lead to breakthrough improvements, it can enhance focus on health system objectives, accountability, and strategic health purchasing. Public recognition of excellence, such as awards or designations, can motivate staff and improve a facility's image, potentially increasing client numbers and revenue. However, compliance must be externally monitored, and the meaning of such designations must be communicated to the public. Public reporting of quality indicators and outcomes is another way to hold facilities accountable and incentivize improvements. Public recognition of adherence to the updated Ten Steps can encourage compliance with Baby-Friendly standards, provided internal and external quality-assurance systems are in place to sustain service quality. National authorities must design these systems to be feasible within available financial and human resources. While the traditional Baby-Friendly model focused on facility designation, public reporting of quality indicators and outcomes offers an alternative approach to encourage improvements in maternity and newborn care facilities.
